evidence.description: How overlapping qualities differ from coincident uncolored lines
Different rankings change outputs for the same derivation
Generalization to materials and scope of the formalism

sections.title: In brief
sections.text: Color grammars extend shape rules with quality-filled regions, allowing geometry and qualities to be generated together.

sections.title: Question
sections.text: What happens when differently colored—or otherwise qualified—regions overlap?

sections.title: Main idea
sections.text: A quality field adds information that bare lines cannot carry. Its overlap needs an explicit convention rather than automatic geometric fusion.

sections.title: Method
sections.text: Add a color-field component to labeled shapes and rules. Rankings determine which coincident qualities dominate or combine, alongside spatial operations.

sections.title: Worked evidence
sections.text: The same rule sequence in Figures 26 and 27 produces different designs under different rankings: one separates into layers, while the other forms a weave.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.text: Color is one example of a more general quality. Knight explains how an overlap convention could also decide material intersections in an architectural design.

sections.title: Limits
sections.text: These are formal constructions and illustrative interpretations, not empirical tests of painting, materials or buildability. The relation between rankings and apparent layering is not straightforward for every grammar.

sections.title: Why read it
sections.text: Color can participate in computation rather than merely decorate the finished drawing. Geometry alone does not settle how overlapping attributes should behave.

terms.meaning: A spatial region supplied with qualities such as color; it may be continuous or disconnected.
A rule for resolving or combining qualities in coincident regions.
